particulars: All names, dates, places, sums, heights, weights, print counts, point counts, sentence lengths and court names were dropped.

items.record: The case is a criminal prosecution of one man for armed robbery: "charged him with two counts of armed robbery".
items.reading: A state body publishes an official review of harm to families in a child-welfare or institutional-care setting.
items.loss: The basic nature of the matter is wrong: it is an individual wrongful conviction, not an institution reviewing its own past conduct.

items.record: The contested account is a forensic report by one police examiner that falsely claimed a search had been done: "Babb had never run the prints through SAFIS in 2014: they were loaded but never searched, although his report said they had been."
items.reading: A self-authored institutional report that is accurate sentence by sentence but curated to look closed.
items.loss: The reading misses that the official record contained a specific false statement of procedure, not only a selective framing.

items.record: The conviction rested on two cross-racial eyewitness picks made on a second look, explained by the eyes, against descriptions that did not fit him: "I think it was him... It's his eyes. 80 percent."
items.loss: The mechanism of the error, uncertain eyewitness identification reinforced by a single partial print, is missing.

items.record: A witness said police steered her toward his photo, and she insisted he was innocent: "an officer pointed to Brown's photo and asked whether she was sure it wasn't him"; "I know it's not him."
items.loss: The reading misses police suggestion in the identification process and a witness who contradicted the prosecution.

items.record: The jury split the verdict under pressure: "Judge Henry Hight gave an Allen charge urging a unanimous verdict"; acquitted on one count, convicted on the other.
items.loss: The reading misses a divided jury pushed to unanimity and an inconsistent outcome on two linked charges.

items.record: The physical evidence was destroyed and the claim failed for lack of proof of bad faith: "no due-process violation because there was no proof the clerk had acted in bad faith".
items.reading: The dispute drifts from what happened to who knew, to independence, to what recommendations bind.
items.loss: The reading misses the real sequence: evidence destroyed, a legal challenge lost on the standard of intent, then a shift to other routes.

items.record: The person challenging the record is a single prisoner, joined by an innocence project years after his appeal failed: "The North Carolina Center on Actual Innocence began representing him in 2016."
items.reading: Organized families, survivors, journalists, a parliamentary committee or lawyers contest the account.
items.loss: The reading gets the opposing party wrong: one convicted individual backed by specialist post-conviction lawyers, not a collective of affected families.

items.record: Brown's lawyers had to go around the police to get the facts: "The police department said it had no records... Brown's lawyers confirmed with the State Bureau of Investigation"; "The court ordered the review disclosed."
items.reading: Litigation forcing disclosure is named as one possible path.
items.loss: The reading misses how disclosure actually happened, through court orders, a separate state agency and an internal audit of the examiner.

items.record: The rerun database search pointed to another man: "one of the three prints came from a man identified as Daris J.... who was taller and heavier than Brown".
items.loss: The reading misses that new forensic searching identified an alternative suspect, which is what decided the case.

items.record: The case ended in full relief: "The state consented to a new trial"; "the state dismissed the charge against Brown."
items.reading: Full resolution is unlikely; partial resolution such as a second review, an apology or a settlement is likely, and the original report keeps its weight.
items.loss: The outcome is wrong: the conviction was vacated and the charge dropped, although the state still denied that the trial lawyer was at fault.

items.record: Brown had already served his time and been released before he was cleared: "While his motions were being heard, Brown was released from prison."
items.loss: The reading misses the order of events: punishment was completed years before exoneration.

items.record: The family aspect is a single father with custody of his son: "I had a full-time job and custody of my son."
items.reading: "Family overlay" is read as families harmed collectively by an institution.
items.loss: The reading misdescribes the family dimension as collective institutional harm rather than one parent's personal situation offered in his own defence.
